name: Hibiscus (roselle, Hibiscus sabdariffa)
short: Case reports: severe INR rise on warfarin after hibiscus tea (possible interaction); skin toxicity with erlotinib. Animal studies: altered captopril, diuretic levels. Trials: no excess adverse events.
text: An overview of reviews with an updated meta-analysis found, from 26 randomised controlled trials (1797 participants), that Hibiscus sabdariffa lowered systolic and diastolic blood pressure compared with placebo and other teas, with effects the authors called comparable to antihypertensive drugs; it also found a minor, clinically insignificant increase in the liver enzyme aspartate aminotransferase, without a higher risk of adverse events; the authors wrote that hibiscus is generally considered safe but that the safety of long-term and therapeutic doses requires careful monitoring. A case report, titled as a severe rise in INR, describes a 59-year-old woman with a mechanical mitral valve on long-term warfarin who developed a markedly elevated INR after recently drinking hibiscus tea, with no other clear cause identified; the authors describe a possible interaction between warfarin and hibiscus products. Two case-report letters without abstracts are titled "Cutaneous Toxicity Induced by Hibiscus Tea in a Patient Treated with Erlotinib" and "The role of flavonoids in false positive digoxin assays caused by the consumption of hibiscus flower and rose hip tea" (the second involves a tea combined with rose hip). In animal studies, hibiscus extract given with the diuretic hydrochlorothiazide to rats and rabbits increased urine volume and raised and prolonged the drug's blood levels, which the authors called a possible herb-drug interaction, and two weeks of a hibiscus water extract given by mouth to rats sharply reduced blood levels of the blood-pressure medicine captopril, and the authors concluded that taking the hibiscus extract together with captopril should be avoided.
